rendered:
No. The paper reports no head-to-head comparison against PCR or blood culture on the clinical samples. Culture and PCR come up only in the introduction, as current methods for identifying pathogens: bacterial culture [5] and polymerase chain reaction [6]are widely employed for pathogen iden-tification[1]. The authors present these methods as background, saying they are often time-consuming and require specialized expertise[2]. They are not used as reference methods. PCR also appears in the title of a cited reference, but not in the methods or results.

For the clinical test, serum was collected from septic patients with confirmed E. coli infection, septic patients with confirmed E. faecium infection, and healthy volunteers serving as the control[3]. The paper does not say how those infections were confirmed. The only result reported is that the sensor array separated the groups in an LDA score plot (Fig. 5[4]), where the plotted points are technical replicates[5]. The paper reports no agreement statistics against another method, such as sensitivity or concordance with a reference test. It also never mentions blood culture or qPCR.[6]
